newsitem.title: USA: Sun shines as management changes bear fruit.
newsitem.headline: Sun shines as management changes bear fruit.

text.p: Management changes at Phildelphia-based refiner Sun Co bore fruit in the second quarter when earnings more than doubled, pushing its shares up over five percent, while the wider market languished.
Philadelphia-based Sun said on Wednesday that operating income surged to $105 million, or 1.07 per share, from $50 million, or $0.50 a year ago.
This prompted Oppenheimer analyst Bruce Lanni to raise his 1997 earnings per share estimate to $2.55 from $2.13 for 1997 and increase his target price for the stock to $38.
Sun was trading up 1-3/4 at 32-7/8 by 1400 EDT.
"The company did this without the help of improved margins, the bottom line is that we are now looking at a new company," said Lanni.

Last November, Sun appointed Jack Drosdick, formerly chief executive at refiner Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp, as its chief executive and the benefits of this are now feeding through to the bottom line, despit a $0.45 per barrel decline in refining margins.

The company pushed its refineries harder than a year ago running them at 104 percent of nameplate capacity and its Northeast refining, marketing and chemicals division saw earnings jump $54 million to $76 million.
Production in the Northeast was up by 2.5 million barrels and gasoline and distillate production averaged over 424,000 barrels daily versus 376,000 in the second quarter of 1996.
"On the cost side, cash refinery expenses were lower by $25 million and total unit expenses were reduced by $35 million," Drosdick said.
"The company is way ahead on its cost cutting and achieved this result with no help from margins," said analyst Lanni.
Sun also said that it would also buy back $150 million in shares.
ABN AMRO First Chicago analyst Eugene Nowak said that he had raised his earnings per share forecast to $2.75 from $1.75 for this year.
"They can keep going forward, but probably not at the fantastic rate we saw in this quarter," Nowak said.
Another refiner, Tosco Corp, also reported and at $0.43 per share earnings were in line with forecasts.
The company, which is the largest independent refiner in the U.S., said that earnings were hurt by acquisitions and weak refining margins on the West Coast.
"Long term, this company is an excellent story, but they are now having to face up to the problems of being a big company," said Oppenheimer's Lanni.

Tosco last year bought 2,500 convenience stores from Circle K last year and is currently in the throes of digesting its new 76 Products assets from Unocal Corp, of which it has already sold $60 million in assets.
The company said that startup expenses at its Trainer, Pa, refinery had reduced earnings by $12 million so far this year.
Despite the acquisitions, Tosco's chief executive, Thomas O'Malley remains on the lookout for more.
The company recently undertook a $700 million equity offering, which it used to purchase stock back from Unocal.
"Tosco's financial strength and flexibility should leave the Company well-positioned to take advantage of whatever opportunities the market may bring," O'Malley said.
((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
